immigrants addressed. In the words of the Justice Department’s Office of 
Legal Counsel, deferred action “refers to an exercise of administrative 
discretion in which immigration officials temporarily defer the removal of 
an alien unlawfully present in the United States.” Though the practice 
“developed without express statutory authorization, it has become a 
regular feature of the immigration removal system that has been 
acknowledged by both Congress and the Supreme Court.” A grant of 
deferred action “does not estabhsh any enforceable legal right to remain in 
the United States” and “may be revoked by immigration authorities at their 
discretion.” But if not revoked, “it represents DHS’s decision not to seek the 
aHen’s removal for a specified period of time.” DHS’s predecessor agency 
promulgated rules by notice and comment (still in force) that make 
grantees of deferred action eligible for certain benefits that DHS has 
statutory authority to confer, including the opportunity to apply for 
authorization to work in the United States if certain criteria are met. 
“Immigration officials today continue to grant deferred action in individual 
cases for humanitarian and other purposes,” a practice known as “ad hoc 
deferred action.” Besides this, DHS and its predecessor have, over the last 
few decades, sometimes adopted policies that made deferred action 
available to generically defined classes of persons. Memorandum from the 
Office of Legal Counsel to the Secretary of Homeland Security and the 
Counsel to the President 10—14 (Nov. 19, 2014) (internal quotation marks 
and citations omitted). In 2012-14, DHS under President Obama adopted 
policies of this type that generated extraordinary political and legal 
controversy, evidenced in the opinion below.
